questions.stem: A child with leukemia is receiving chemotherapy. Which instruction should the nurse give the parents?

options.text: Avoid live vaccines and crowds, and report any fever right away
Keep all immunizations on schedule, including live vaccines
A fever is expected and can be ignored

rationale.correct: Leukemia: infection and bleeding precautions, no live vaccines, report fever immediately.

perOption.a: The child is immunosuppressed.
perOption.b: Live vaccines are contraindicated during chemotherapy.
perOption.c: Rectal temperatures risk injury and infection.
perOption.d: Fever may signal a serious infection.

references: Pediatric nursing texts (e.g. Hockenberry, Wong's Essentials of Pediatric Nursing)

questions.educationalObjective: Teach infection precautions for a child with leukemia.

questions.stem: A 2-year-old with sickle cell disease suddenly becomes pale and lethargic, with a rapidly enlarging spleen and a rapid heart rate. What does the nurse suspect?

rationale.correct: Splenic sequestration: pallor, an enlarging spleen and hypovolemic shock; transfusion is needed.

perOption.a: Blood pools in the spleen, causing shock; this is an emergency.
perOption.b: This causes pain, not an enlarging spleen with shock.

references: Pediatric nursing texts (e.g. Hockenberry, Wong's Essentials of Pediatric Nursing)

questions.stem: A 2-year-old drinks about 1.4 L (48 oz) of cow's milk a day and eats little solid food. Which condition is this child at risk for?

rationale.correct: Limit milk to about 470 to 710 mL (16 to 24 oz) a day for toddlers and offer iron-rich foods.

perOption.a: Too much milk displaces iron-rich foods and can cause GI blood loss.
perOption.d: Iron deficiency is the main concern.

questions.stem: A child has a high blood lead level and is starting chelation therapy. Which intervention is important?

options.text: Maintain good hydration and monitor kidney function
Stop the therapy if urine output increases

rationale.correct: Lead poisoning: remove the source, chelation as needed and monitor the kidneys.

perOption.a: Chelated lead is excreted in the urine and can stress the kidneys.

options.text: When all lesions have crusted over
When the first new lesion appears

rationale.correct: Varicella: airborne and contact precautions until all lesions crust; avoid contact with pregnant or immunocompromised people.

perOption.a: Varicella is contagious until all lesions are crusted.
perOption.b: The child may still be contagious.
perOption.d: This is when contagiousness is high.

questions.stem: For each childhood illness, indicate its characteristic finding.

columns.text: Vesicles in different stages at the same time
Small white spots on the inside of the cheeks
High fever for 3 days, then a rash as the fever breaks

rationale.correct: Know the hallmark findings of common childhood rashes.

perOption.r1:c1: Crops of lesions in different stages are typical.
perOption.r1:c2: These are Koplik spots of measles.
perOption.r2:c2: Koplik spots appear before the measles rash.
perOption.r3:c3: The slapped-cheek rash is typical of parvovirus B19.
perOption.r4:c4: The rash appears as the high fever ends.

questions.stem: A child is diagnosed with scabies. Which instruction should the nurse give?

options.text: Treat all household members with permethrin at the same time and wash bedding in hot water
Treat only the child with symptoms
Expect the itching to stop the same day
Keep using the same unwashed bedding

rationale.correct: Scabies: treat all contacts, wash linens in hot water or bag them for 72 hours or more.

perOption.a: This prevents reinfestation.
perOption.b: Others may be infested without symptoms.

questions.stem: Which finding most strongly suggests physical abuse?

options.text: A spiral fracture of the femur in a 4-month-old who can't yet crawl
Bruises on the shins of a 4-year-old
A scraped knee in a school-age child
A forehead bump in a toddler learning to walk

rationale.correct: Red flags: injuries that don't fit the child's development or the history, patterned injuries and delays in seeking care.

perOption.a: Spiral fractures in an infant who can't move independently suggest twisting injuries.
perOption.b: Shin bruises are common in active children.

references: Pediatric nursing texts (e.g. Hockenberry, Wong's Essentials of Pediatric Nursing)
